plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-part illustration of a bouncing light pulse seen from two reference frames. Part (a) shows a side view of a space shuttle above a magnified inset: inside a rounded frame an astronaut in an orange suit, labeled Astronaut, floats beside an analog clock reading delta tau, while a Light source drawn as a yellow burst and a Receiver sit side by side beneath a Mirror, with teal arrows carrying the pulse straight up and straight back down over the bracketed vertical distance D. Part (b) shows the same apparatus from outside: three dashed-outline snapshots of the cabin run left to right, and a purple path labeled s goes diagonally up from the source in the left snapshot, labeled Beginning event, to the mirror in the middle snapshot, then down as a second segment s to the receiver in the right snapshot, labeled Ending event. Brackets below give the horizontal shifts L = v delta t / 2 and L, and a standing figure on a tan ground plane is labeled Observer on Earth beside a clock reading delta t. Part (c) reduces the picture to bare geometry, an isosceles triangle whose two slanted sides are each labeled s, divided by a vertical altitude D into right triangles with bases L = v delta t / 2 and L, with s = sqrt(D squared + L squared) written above. Drawing the same pair of events twice makes the two path lengths directly comparable, which is what forces the two recorded times apart.

interactionPlan.concept: The same light-clock events have a vertical path in the astronaut's frame and a longer diagonal path in Earth's frame, so the moving clock's elapsed time is dilated by geometry.

interactions.label: Observer frame
interactions.teaches: The astronaut measures the light going straight up and down a total distance 2D, while the Earth observer measures the same two events connected by two longer diagonal segments 2s

interactions.label: Shuttle speed v/c
interactions.teaches: Increasing the shuttle speed increases the horizontal displacement L, lengthens the diagonal light path s, and makes the Earth-frame time Δt larger compared with the astronaut's proper time Δτ

interactions.label: Step through light pulse
interactions.teaches: The beginning, reflection, and ending are the same events in both frames; observers disagree about the path length and elapsed time, not about which events occurred

demo_steps.title: Start in the astronaut's frame
demo_steps.narration: Inside the shuttle, the light source, mirror, and receiver are at rest with the astronaut. The pulse travels straight up and straight back down, so the clock in this frame records the proper time Δτ.

demo_steps.title: Follow the same events from Earth
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the Earth observer: while the light is in flight, the shuttle moves horizontally. The same beginning, reflection, and ending events now form two diagonal light paths instead of a vertical round trip.

demo_steps.title: Complete the pulse trip
demo_steps.narration: At the ending event, the pulse reaches the receiver. Both observers agree that emission, reflection, and reception happened, but the Earth observer assigns the light a longer path, 2s rather than 2D.

demo_steps.title: Increase the shuttle speed
demo_steps.narration: Drag the speed slider upward: the cabin snapshots spread apart, L grows, and the purple diagonal sides of the triangle lengthen. Because light speed is the same for both observers, the longer Earth-frame path requires a larger elapsed time Δt.

demo_steps.title: Connect the picture to the triangle
demo_steps.narration: The reduced triangle shows the whole argument: each half-trip has vertical leg D, horizontal leg L = vΔt/2, and hypotenuse s. Since s = √(D² + L²), any nonzero horizontal motion makes s greater than D.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Time dilation follows from one geometric fact: in the Earth frame the same light pulse travels a longer diagonal distance while still moving at speed c, so the measured time must be longer.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean three-panel SVG layout echoing the original: astronaut-frame shuttle inset on the left, Earth-frame dashed cabin snapshots on the right, and a simplified triangle below. In astronaut-frame mode, emphasize the left inset with teal vertical arrows and the Δτ clock while dimming the Earth-frame diagonals; in Earth-frame mode, emphasize the right snapshots, purple diagonal path, Δt clock, and lower triangle. The shuttle speed slider should keep D fixed while increasing horizontal spacing L between snapshots and steepening/lengthening the purple path segments. The event button should place a bright marker at the light source for beginning, at the mirror/apex for reflection, and at the receiver for ending, with matching highlights in the triangle. Preserve the labels D, s, L = vΔt/2, L, Δτ, Δt, Beginning event, Ending event, Astronaut, Observer on Earth, Light source, Receiver, and Mirror.

authoredContext:
The analysis of simultaneity shows that Einstein’s postulates imply an important effect: Time intervals have different values when measured in different inertial frames. Suppose, for example, an astronaut measures the time it takes for a pulse of light to travel a distance perpendicular to the direction of his ship’s motion (relative to an earthbound observer), bounce off a mirror, and return (the figure). How does the elapsed time that the astronaut measures in the spacecraft compare with the elapsed time that an earthbound observer measures by observing what is happening in the spacecraft?

Examining this question leads to a profound result. The elapsed time for a process depends on which observer is measuring it. In this case, the time measured by the astronaut (within the spaceship where the astronaut is at rest) is smaller than the time measured by the earthbound observer (to whom the astronaut is moving). The time elapsed for the same process is different for the observers, because the distance the light pulse travels in the astronaut’s frame is smaller than in the earthbound frame, as seen in the figure. Light travels at the same speed in each frame, so it takes more time to travel the greater distance in the earthbound frame.

To quantitatively compare the time measurements in the two inertial frames, we can relate the distances in the figure to each other, then express each distance in terms of the time of travel (respectively either Δt or Δτ) of the pulse in the corresponding reference frame. The resulting equation can then be solved for Δt in terms of Δτ.

The lengths D and L in the figure are the sides of a right triangle with hypotenuse s. From the Pythagorean theorem,

(a) An astronaut measures the time Δτ for light to travel distance 2D in the astronaut’s frame. (b) A NASA scientist on Earth sees the light follow the longer path 2s and take a longer time Δt. (c) These triangles are used to find the relationship between the two distances D and s.

Figure a shows an illustration of an astronaut in the space shuttle observing an analog clock with an elapsed time Delta tau. The details of the clock experiment are also shown as follows: There is a light source, a receiver a short distance to its right, and a mirror centered above them. The vertical distance from the receiver and light source to the mirror is labeled as D. The path of the light from the source, up to the mirror, and back down to the receiver is shown. Figure b shows an observer on earth with an analog clock showing a time interval Delta t. Above the observer are three diagrams showing the clock experiment on the space shuttle at three different times and the path of the light. The light source in the diagram on the left is labeled “beginning event.” The receiver in the diagram on the right is labeled “ending event.” The path of the light forms a straight line going diagonally up and to the right, from the source in the diagram on the left to the mirror in the center diagram, and then another straight line going diagonally down and to the right, from the mirror in the center diagram to the receiver in the diagram on the right. The vertical distance from the receiver to the mirror is labeled D. The horizontal distance from the beginning event to the clock location in the center diagram is labeled L= v Delta t over 2. The horizontal distance from the clock location in the center diagram to the ending event is labeled L. Figure c shows an isosceles triangle with a horizontal base. The triangle is divided by a vertical line from its apex to its base into two identical right triangles with the vertical line forming a side that is shared by the two right triangles. This side is labeled D. The base of the triangle on the left is labeled L= v Delta t over 2. The base of the triangle on the right is labeled L. The hypotenuse of each of the right triangles is labeled s. Above the diagram is the equation s equals the square root of the quantity D squared plus L squared.

event: beginning Inside the shuttle, the light source, mirror, and receiver are at rest with the astronaut. The pulse travels straight up and straight back down, so the clock in this frame records the proper time Δτ.
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: The default state heavily fades panels (b) and (c) behind a white dimmer overlay, whereas the source figure shows all three panels at full contrast as a static textbook diagram.
The large translucent beam connecting the shuttle to the enlarged cabin inset is missing; the generated version uses only two thin connector lines, changing the composition of panel (a).

Several labels are rendered much smaller and fainter than in the source, especially in the Earth-frame snapshots, event labels, observer label, and triangle labels, making them hard to read at inline size.

The fraction labels are not faithfully typeset: 'L = v Δt / 2' is approximated as stacked plain text without a fraction bar, and the triangle equation is simplified to 's = √ D² + L²' without the radical bar over the full expression.
The speed-dependent geometry is not conceptually exact: at v/c = 0 the code still gives a nonzero horizontal distance L, so the Earth-frame diagonal path and triangle do not collapse correctly.
evaluation.notes: The main light-clock panels, snapshots, triangle, and labels are recognizable and the interactions are useful, but the default dimming, weak label legibility, missing inset beam, and nonzero L at zero speed reduce its value as a drop-in replacement.
action_items: Make the default view match the static source by showing panels (a), (b), and (c) at full opacity, reserving dimming/highlighting only after the user activates a step or frame emphasis.
Add the broad translucent trapezoidal beam from the shuttle down to the rounded inset, not just two thin connector lines.
Increase label size and contrast in panels (b) and (c), especially the event labels, observer label, s/D/L labels, and formula text.
Use proper fraction-style labels with a visible horizontal bar for L = vΔt/2, and typeset s = √(D² + L²) with clearer grouping.
plan_action_items: Revise the speed-to-geometry mapping so L is proportional to v and becomes zero when v/c = 0; otherwise the slider teaches an incorrect limiting case.

interactions.label: Observer frame
interactions.teaches: The astronaut measures the light going straight up and down a total distance 2D, while the Earth observer measures the same two events connected by two longer diagonal segments 2s

interactions.label: Shuttle speed v/c
interactions.teaches: Increasing the shuttle speed increases the horizontal displacement L, lengthens the diagonal light path s, and makes the Earth-frame time Δt larger compared with the astronaut's proper time Δτ

interactions.label: Step through light pulse
interactions.teaches: The beginning, reflection, and ending are the same events in both frames; observers disagree about the path length and elapsed time, not about which events occurred

demo_steps.title: Start in the astronaut's frame
demo_steps.narration: Inside the shuttle, the light source, mirror, and receiver are at rest with the astronaut. The pulse travels straight up and straight back down, so the clock in this frame records the proper time Δτ.

demo_steps.title: Follow the same events from Earth
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the Earth observer: while the light is in flight, the shuttle moves horizontally. The same beginning, reflection, and ending events now form two diagonal light paths instead of a vertical round trip.

demo_steps.title: Complete the pulse trip
demo_steps.narration: At the ending event, the pulse reaches the receiver. Both observers agree that emission, reflection, and reception happened, but the Earth observer assigns the light a longer path, 2s rather than 2D.

demo_steps.title: Increase the shuttle speed
demo_steps.narration: Drag the speed slider upward: the cabin snapshots spread apart, L grows, and the purple diagonal sides of the triangle lengthen. Because light speed is the same for both observers, the longer Earth-frame path requires a larger elapsed time Δt.

demo_steps.title: Connect the picture to the triangle
demo_steps.narration: The reduced triangle shows the whole argument: each half-trip has vertical leg D, horizontal leg L = vΔt/2, and hypotenuse s. Since s = √(D² + L²), any nonzero horizontal motion makes s greater than D.

plan.keyInsight: Time dilation follows from one geometric fact: in the Earth frame the same light pulse travels a longer diagonal distance while still moving at speed c, so the measured time must be longer.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean three-panel SVG layout echoing the original: astronaut-frame shuttle inset on the left, Earth-frame dashed cabin snapshots on the right, and a simplified triangle below. In astronaut-frame mode, emphasize the left inset with teal vertical arrows and the Δτ clock while dimming the Earth-frame diagonals; in Earth-frame mode, emphasize the right snapshots, purple diagonal path, Δt clock, and lower triangle. The shuttle speed slider should keep D fixed while increasing horizontal spacing L between snapshots and steepening/lengthening the purple path segments. The event button should place a bright marker at the light source for beginning, at the mirror/apex for reflection, and at the receiver for ending, with matching highlights in the triangle. Preserve the labels D, s, L = vΔt/2, L, Δτ, Δt, Beginning event, Ending event, Astronaut, Observer on Earth, Light source, Receiver, and Mirror.
